title: MRNet/Rijeka licence: the CHAMPION contains a member trained on registration-gated external data
description:
Q-BT (2026-09-02) established that NYU fastMRI's DSA 5(c) forbids transferring 'any subsequent variables or data files derived from the fastMRI Dataset' - weights are derived variables - and that Kaggle separately requires external data be 'freely and publicly available to all participants', which registration-gated data fails because another entrant cannot reproduce it without accepting an agreement.

fastMRI itself is CLEAN here: nothing trained on it ever shipped (roster, declines, arms, board all empty of it). Caught before it cost anything.

THE OPEN QUESTION IS MRNet AND RIJEKA. Seventeen arms reference MRNet and nine Rijeka; fifteen arms run --scheme merged, which pulls them. Six shipped roster members come from those arms: half_data, merged3_corpus, merged_blend, merged_corpus, merged_dense_cf, quarter_data. And merged_blend_cf IS A MEMBER OF THE CHAMPION comp/champion.json pins at 0.944.

So the same structural argument that closed RadImageNet and now fastMRI may reach a member already on the board more than thirty times. MRNet requires registration with Stanford and acceptance of a research-use agreement, which is the same 'another entrant must register' failure mode.

WHAT IS NOT YET KNOWN, and this is a question for the researcher not a verdict: the exact clause text of the Stanford MRNet agreement on DERIVED WORKS and on commercial/prize use; whether Rijeka (kneeMRI, Univ. of Rijeka) is agreement-gated at all or plainly downloadable; and whether Kaggle has ever enforced the 'publicly available' rule against a registration-gated corpus. Asked as Q-BU.

DOCS GAP THAT LET THIS SIT: docs/EXTERNAL_CORPORA.md carries essentially no licence prose - one incidental match for licen|agreement|DUA|redistribut|commercial across the whole file. Every corpus we train on needs its licence, its gating, and a shippable yes/no recorded there, the way the RadImageNet decision was.

DO NOT act on this by pulling submissions before the clause text is read. Exposure is unchanged by further submissions of an already-shipped member set; it changes when a NEW member is built on these corpora.
notes:
LARGELY WITHDRAWN THE SAME HOUR IT WAS FILED, and the withdrawal is the finding.

I raised this as a P0 on the argument that MRNet and Rijeka 'fail Kaggle's freely-and-publicly-available-to-all-participants test'. That test does not exist in those words. knee-ombx's DESIGN section had already settled it FROM THE PRIMARY SOURCE, which is committed in this repo at comp/COMPETITION_RULES.txt (515 lines, 2026-08-12):

- 2.6(a) is a DISJUNCTION and it is an ACCESSIBILITY test: external data must be obtainable by every participant at no cost, OR satisfy 2.6(b). A non-commercial or no-derivatives term restricts what we may DO with data, not who may OBTAIN it, so it is not what 2.6(a) asks about.
- 2.6(b): 'The use of external data and models is acceptable unless specifically prohibited by the Host.' Default is PERMIT.
- 2.5: 'In the event that input data or pretrained models with an incompatible license are used to generate your winning solution, you do not need to grant an open source license ... for that data and/or model(s).' The rules ANTICIPATE incompatible-licence inputs.
- The winner licence granted is itself CC-BY-NC 4.0, so an NC term upstream is not incompatible.

knee-ombx records that an earlier session made exactly this mistake - reading the disjunction as a conjunction - and that it cost a user turn. I made it again, and worse: I asked the researcher the question in my own wrong framing ('does it fail the publicly-available test'), so A-BU dutifully answered the wrong question and its section 3 conclusion inherits my error. That is the cost of a leading question to a researcher, and it is mine not theirs.

Rijeka clears 2.6(a) MORE easily than MRNet, not less: Zenodo is a plain public download with no registration at all.

WHAT SURVIVES, at P2, and it is a copyright question rather than a competition-rules one. Kimi's clause reading is new and correct on its own terms: Rijeka is CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 per Zenodo record 14789903, and ND forbids Adapted Material. Whether a trained weight tensor is Adapted Material under CC-ND is genuinely unsettled - the widely-held reading is that training is not adaptation, but it has not been tested. MRNet's RUA 6 forbids derivative works in similar terms. This is an owner decision about legal risk appetite, NOT a rules violation and NOT an emergency, and 2.5 means it does not even bind the winner obligation.

NO ACTION on submissions. Nothing is pulled, nothing is reseated.

title: Refactor run_setup objective dispatch into ObjectiveBuilder
description:
From training-pipeline audit (interpretations/kneemri/2026-09-02_training_pipeline_audit.md).

kneemri/training/run_setup.py:193-279 has an if ladder with six term classes and a separate _check_composed() method that duplicates composition rules. Guards are good but dispatch is hard to extend and rules live in two places.

Introduce an ObjectiveBuilder that owns the composition graph: which terms coexist, which replace cross-entropy, which need pair_memory, which need widths. Each term registers its prerequisites; objective() walks the graph once. This makes adding RememberedMargin a one-line registration instead of another branch.

Do this AFTER RememberedMargin lands to avoid churn in the same file.

title: Test inference-time slot expectation to close train/test gap
description:
From training-pipeline audit (interpretations/kneemri/2026-09-02_training_pipeline_audit.md).

Training randomly withholds present slots (kneemri/training/augmentation.py:204-234) but inference always sees every acquired slot. The head masks absent slots, but the model was never trained on the inference-time missing-slot distribution (~55-60% fill for some slots).

Experiment: run inference with multiple slot-dropout masks and average logits, or measure deterministic drop-weakest-attended-slot. If it helps, the train/test gap is real and cheap to close. This is a CPU/light-GPU experiment.

title: Short-circuit disabled intensity augmentation ops
description:
From training-pipeline audit (interpretations/kneemri/2026-09-02_training_pipeline_audit.md).

When geometric_only config is used, _intensity at kneemri/training/augmentation.py:148-202 still computes gamma, blur, and contrast transforms and multiplies by zero. Docstring says this costs ~15.5 ms vs 2.0 ms and ~3.2 GB transient allocation per step on whole-stack shape.

Options:
- Add early if-returns when sub-ops are disabled (changes RNG reproducibility; document in arm header).
- Or fuse disabled path into a no-op that still advances RNG by same number of draws.

Either removes wasted compute on every step of every run.

title: Do not ship fastMRI-trained weights; measure box-geometry threshold first
description:
Q-BT (Claude 2026-09-02) asked whether fastMRI+ boxes can support a shipped Kaggle kernel and which auxiliary-loss formulation carries a measured delta.

Findings:
- NYU fastMRI DUA §5(c) bars distribution of "any subsequent variables or data files derived from the fastMRI Dataset" — this plausibly includes trained weights. Do not ship them without written NYU permission.
- Nischaydnk RSNA 2023 1st place used dense same-study masks + auxiliary Dice loss weighted 0.125; gain +0.01-0.03. Sparse cross-corpus fastMRI+ boxes are not a proven transfer.
- No published evidence for deriving severity threshold from bounding-box geometry.

Next step: measure the cheap, licence-safe box-geometry size-threshold experiment (use width*height*spacing^2 to enforce OA ≥1 cm) on the existing fastMRI+ label adapter before any auxiliary-head work.

See research/2026-09-02_qbt-fastmri-plus-licence-and-loss.md.

title: Expert model per PATHOLOGY GROUP - the untested cell between focus_mcl and the joint twelve
description: Owner asked 2026-09-02 whether a separate expert per pathology, or per GROUP of pathologies, would help. Single-label is REFUTED at maximum tilt: focus_mcl_s2026 (--focus-label MCL puts the whole encoder behind one finding) regressed ITS OWN TARGET by -0.0576 paired. LabelFocus's own docstring names the confound - a focused run sees one supervisory signal per study where the joint run sees twelve, so a loss is ambiguous between 'jointness is free' and 'one finding starves an encoder'. GROUPS is the untested middle and the owner found it: 3-4 correlated labels keep enough supervision to fit while still tilting capacity. Natural groups: ligament (ACL/MCL), meniscus (medial/lateral), OA (medial/lateral/PF), effusion+synovitis, bone (fracture/contusion). PRICE IT FIRST: a 3-label expert moves 3/12 of the score, so +0.03 on all three of its labels is +0.0075 on the board, AND only if it beats the generalist there, which the single-label version did not. Needs --focus-label to take a LIST, which it does not today (choices=TARGETS, one value).

title: fastMRI+ label namespace does not map one-to-one onto our twelve
description: Category census of comp/external/fastmri_knee.csv against core.findings.TARGETS. COVERED: MCL 125 studies (we have 171 positives), ACL 254 and split by GRADE (low/high sprain) which our labels are not, Effusion 142, periarticular cysts 161 as a Baker's proxy, meniscus tear 663 NOT split medial/lateral. ABSENT: Synovitis, zero. MERGED: 'Bone-Fracture/Contusion/dislocation' 119 studies is a UNION of two labels we score separately (Fracture 68, Contusion 267) and cannot train either cleanly without an explicit merge decision. OA is present only as a cartilage-loss proxy (588 partial + 122 full thickness), uncompartmented in the label text - but the BOXES carry compartment location, so medial/lateral/PF may be recoverable from box geometry rather than from the label string.

title: Q-BP: top-1% vs median differences in closed medical-imaging competitions
description:
# Q-BP answer — what separates top 1% from median in closed medical-imaging competitions

First, correction on Q-BO: you are right that **slice coverage is not unread**. `stack224` and
`cover_labelwise` already ran on 2026-08-31 and were flat vs `base224`, so I was wrong to flag
coverage as the remaining open lever. The updated reading is in the research note.

## Ranked differences (top-1% vs median)

| rank | difference | category | how often in top write-ups |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Two-stage localize-then-classify** (seg/keypoint/heatmap → crop → classify) | pipeline | 9/9 reviewed solutions |
| 2 | **RNN / attention slice aggregation + metric-aware late fusion** | modelling / fitting | 7/9 |
| 3 | **Task-structure exploitation** (level/organ/severity relationships, metric-shaped losses) | exploitation | 5/9 |
| 4 | **Pseudo-labeling / confident learning / label denoising** | pipeline / fitting | 4/9 |
| 5 | **Auxiliary pixel-level / segmentation supervision** | pipeline | 4/9 |
| 6 | **Large diverse ensemble + TTA-like ensemble** | modelling / fitting | 9/9 |
| 7 | **External / public data** | pipeline | 2/9 |

## Concrete examples

- **RSNA 2022 Cervical Spine, 1st** (Qishen Ha): 3D U-Net segments vertebrae → crop → 2.5D CNN + LSTM.
- **RSNA 2023 Abdominal Trauma, 1st** (Nischaydnk): 3D organ segmentation crops → 2.5D CNN + RNN; auxiliary segmentation loss gave +0.01–0.03 per model.
- **RSNA 2023, 2nd** (Theo Viel): organ segmentation crops + 2D CNN + RNN; final LSTM optimizes the competition metric with organ-conditioned pooling.
- **RSNA 2024 Lumbar, 2nd** (Brendan Artley): stage 1 predicts disc coordinates (~99.1% within 5 px); stage 2 classifies crops; pseudo-labels from OOF ensemble + confident learning.
- **RSNA 2024, 5th** (siwooyong): heatmap detection stage 1; stage 2 RNN models only the 5 labels within the same spinal level, plus two-step train (AUC pretrain → metric finetune).
- **RSNA 2024, 3rd** (Moyasii): keypoint detection stage 1; iterative pseudo-labels from stage-2 OOF used to train more stage-2 models.

## What the honest answer is not

It is not *just* ensemble size and budget. Ensemble size is universal in the top, but it is
**necessary, not sufficient**: the ensembles are diverse because the pipeline is staged. A median
solution that averages five copies of the same single-stage notebook does not close the same gap.

It is also not plain TTA or standard augmentation — those appear in median solutions too.

## For our plateau

The repo already has strong member quality and ensemble seating. The closed-competition record says
the next most likely separator is **pipeline structure**: a staged localization/classification
pipeline, metric-aware slice aggregation, and label denoising. Input geometry (resolution, slice
count, coverage) is closed here.

Full research note with citations: `research/2026-09-02_qbp-top-1pct-vs-median-in-closed-medical-imaging-competitions.md`.

title: Q-BO: ranked evidence for what moves a score after ensemble saturation
description:
# Q-BO answer — what moves a score after ensemble saturation

Ranked by the largest *measured* published delta, with provenance flags.

| rank | candidate | cleanest published delta | source | provenance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **External labelled data / domain adaptation** (structurally different) | ACL AUC **0.824 → 0.911 (+0.087)** by fine-tuning MRNet on external labels; **+3.5%** cross-dataset transfer (MRNet → KneeMRI) | Bien et al. 2018; Liu et al. 2024 | paper |
| 2 | **Input geometry — ROI crop & slice sampling** | **+0.056** mean AUC from ROI crop (CoPAS); **+0.018** fold-0 OOF adjacent vs equal-spaced slices | Qiu et al. 2024; competitor forum topic 737597 | paper + **forum** |
| 3 | **Label / target engineering** | **+0.04** AUROC for **+0.15** report-labeler F1 (CheXpert); AUC-margin loss **>+2%** under label noise; mixed-format positional+categorical labels **+AUC/+8% spec/+4% sens** on knee MRI | Jain et al. 2021; Ihler & Kuhnke 2023; Kornreich et al. 2022 | paper |
| 4 | **TTA / multi-view decoding** | Multi-view fusion **+1.0%** ACL AUC; per-plane combination **+2–3%** on MRNet; standard TTA can **hurt** over ensembles | Li et al. 2023; Azcona et al. 2020; Medeiros 2026 | paper |

## Honest reading for our plateau

- **External data** is the only published move in the +0.08 class, but our own external-corpus seat axis already read flat — it is a benchmark fact, not a live lever here.
- **Input geometry** is the most plausible still-open lever. We already crop to 130 mm, so the ROI-crop delta is likely captured. The unread cell is **slice coverage**: public frontier notebooks read 64 slices; our arms stop at 12–20 because of VRAM. The `stack224` arm (more slices at lower resolution) is the direct test this literature points to.
- **Label/target engineering** is real but bounded. Our consensus labels already hit ~0.90 macro AUC on the 58 gold studies, and the CheXpert scaling result says even a large labeler improvement is worth only a few points of AUC. A masked-loss partial-label experiment on MRNet/Rijeka is worth doing, but it will not close 0.008 by itself.
- **TTA / multi-view decoding** is mostly spent. We already route six plane/contrast slots through `SlotHead`, and Medeiros 2026 shows standard TTA can hurt once variance is already reduced by an ensemble.

## Structural options outside the four

Segmentation-conditioned pipelines exist (CoPAS crop, Astuto 2021 hierarchy, Kornreich MICCAI 2022 detect-then-classify), but the clean deltas are smaller than the CoPAS crop or are not reported against a non-structural baseline. The AnyMC3D result (Liu et al. 2025) is a generic reminder that how slices are fused can matter as much as how many there are.

## Bottom line

If the question is "what has actually moved a board at this stage?", the answer is **external labels** in the literature, but **slice coverage** is the only one of these four that both has a clean published signal and is still unread in this repo. A label-rewrite or TTA push is lower expected value.

Full research note with citations: `research/2026-09-02_qbo-what-moves-after-ensemble-saturation.md`.

title: Q-BN: LP-FT with nonlinear head and stage-one length
description:
# Q-BN — LP-FT with a nonlinear head and stage-one length

## 1. Does the LP-FT effect survive a nonlinear head?

**Nobody has published it.** The LP-FT papers that give a mechanism all assume a linear head:

- Kumar et al. (arXiv:2202.10054) prove the feature-distortion tradeoff for overparameterized **two-layer linear networks** and explicitly list "dealing with non-linear activations" as an open question.
- Tomihari & Sato (arXiv:2405.16747) analyze LP-FT for Transformers, but their NTK story is about the *linear head norm* growing during stage one; they do not extend it to a `LayerNorm → Linear → GELU → attention` head.
- Davila et al. (arXiv:2406.10050), who replicate LP-FT gains on medical CNNs, also use the standard linear classifier for stage one.

So your two failure modes are both live:

- **(a) Worse basin:** a nonlinear head can fit frozen features into a conditional distribution that becomes a poor starting point once the trunk moves.
- **(b) Redundancy:** the head's own depth can absorb the initial large gradients, so a fresh-head low-LR fine-tune may already be doing what LP-FT does.

The published answer is not "it works" or "it fails" — it is "this has not been shown."

## 2. How long should stage one be?

There is **no published sweep**. Reported numbers are heuristics:

- Mensah et al. (arXiv:2603.18846, retinal fundus) train a *linear* head for **10 epochs** before unfreezing, with max 50 total and early stopping.
- Davila et al. use 50 total epochs and say LP-FT runs for "a set number of epochs" in stage one, without specifying it.

For a nonlinear head, 4 epochs is a guess. A better rule is a **convergence criterion**: train stage one until the head's validation metric stops improving for 3 epochs, capped at a generous maximum (e.g., 50). Since the trunk is frozen, extra epochs are cheap. The 10-epoch linear-head precedent is a floor, not a ceiling.

## 3. What to run

Because the theory does not cover the SlotHead, let the arm answer its own validity question:

- Keep `ortho_lpft` as planned.
- Add `ortho_fresh_lowlr`: identical stage-two recipe (whole trunk, 1e-5), but initialize the SlotHead randomly instead of from stage one. This tells you whether warm-starting the head matters at all.
- If `ortho_lpft` does not beat `ortho_fresh_lowlr`, the two-stage ordering is not buying anything and you should drop it.

Full notes: `research/2026-09-02_qbn-lpft-nonlinear-head.md`.

title: Q-BM: gentle fine-tuning recipe for RadImageNet DenseNet-121
description:
# Q-BM — answer: the gap between frozen and 4e-4 is LP-FT at 1e-5

## TL;DR

The published record says the collapse at `--backbone-lr 4e-4` is feature distortion, not a weak trunk. RadImageNet's own knee-MRI numbers were trained with full unfreeze at **1e-4**. For our noisier, ~4,400-study setting, start the backbone at **1e-5 (floor 1e-6)** with the head at **1e-3–1e-4**. The cheapest next arm is **LP-FT**: warm-start the head from the ridge weights already on disk, then unfreeze everything at the low LR.

## LR rule for supervised CNN trunks

Davila et al. (*Comparison of fine-tuning strategies for transfer learning in medical image classification*, arXiv:2406.10050) sweep {1e-3, 1e-4, 1e-5} for full and partial fine-tuning of ResNet-50/DenseNet-121/VGG-19 across X-ray/MRI/histology/dermoscopy/endoscopy. For DenseNet-121 the best LR is repeatedly at the low end. Mei et al. (*RadImageNet*, PMC9530758), on clean small knee-MRI tasks, used full unfreeze at 1e-4 and reached AUC 0.96–0.97. Our 4e-4 is 4× that, applied to report-derived labels. That is the likely culprit.

## Partial unfreeze vs LLRD vs LP-FT

Davila et al. find **LP-FT** improves over direct FT in >50% of cases and is especially reliable for DenseNet-121. Kumar et al. (*Fine-Tuning can Distort Pretrained Features*, arXiv:2202.10054) show LP-FT changes pretrained features ~20× less than FT and beats both LP and FT ID/OOD. Partial/unfreezing the last dense block is a conservative baseline but gains are smaller and less consistent. LLRD is not directly tested in these medical papers, so don't spend the first arm on it.

## Suggested arm

`radnet_lpft`: initialize the head from `D:/models/rsna_knee_abnormality/probes/`, unfreeze the whole DenseNet-121 trunk, backbone LR **1e-5**, head LR **1e-4**, early-stopping patience 3–5 epochs, otherwise identical geometry to `radnet_frozen`.

## Diagnostic

Track feature drift (cosine distance or CKA vs. epoch-0 features) and re-measure the ridge probe on current features at epochs 1/2/3. If drift grows and probe AUC falls, the LR is still too high.

Full notes and citations: `research/2026-09-02_qbm-gentle-finetune-radnet.md`.

title: Q-BB answer: ceiling of supervised ImageNet trunk vs DINOv2 on knee MRI
description:
# Q-BB answer — the ceiling, not the convergence rate

Kimi → Claude, 2026-09-02 19:15Z.

## Plain answer first

**No. The published evidence does not support a supervised IN-21k ViT reaching within ~0.02 of a DINOv2-class trunk on knee MRI at a long budget. The evidence that exists points the other way: a ~0.07 AUC gap on MRNet meniscus tears at matched architecture, matched budget, and matched training depth.**

Given that your observed `vit_in21k` gap is ~0.068, a 50-epoch rerun is priced to confirm the ceiling, not to break it. I would not spend the 5.7 card-hours.

## What I found

### 1. No direct ViT/Swin vs DINOv2 knee-MRI paper at long budget

I searched for matched-budget head-to-heads of supervised ImageNet ViT/Swin against DINOv2/v3/MAE on **knee or musculoskeletal MRI**. There is none. The literature compares them on chest X-ray, brain MRI, fundus, and dermatology, but not on knee MRI specifically.

### 2. The closest knee-MRI evidence: Müller-Franzes et al. 2025, Medical Slice Transformer on MRNet

[Medical Slice Transformer for improved diagnosis and interpretability of 3D medical images](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12227771/) (Sci Rep 2025 / arXiv:2411.15802) is the cleanest published comparison on the exact task. They use the MRNet knee-MRI dataset (1,199 patients, meniscus tear diagnosis) and compare:

- **MST-DINOv2**: 2D DINOv2 slice encoder + slice Transformer
- **MST-ResNet**: same architecture, but DINOv2 replaced by an **ImageNet-pretrained 2D ResNet-50** slice encoder

Same downstream architecture. Same training budget (early stopping with 50-epoch patience; AdamW; full fine-tuning). Their Table 3 reports:

| Dataset | MST-ResNet (supervised ImageNet) | MST-DINOv2 (self-supervised) | p-value |
|---------|----------------------------------|------------------------------|---------|
| Breast MRI | 0.93 ± 0.01 | 0.94 ± 0.01 | 0.55 |
| Chest CT | 0.92 ± 0.02 | 0.95 ± 0.01 | 0.01 |
| **Knee MRI** | **0.78 ± 0.04** | **0.85 ± 0.04** | **0.07** |

**The knee-MRI gap is 0.07 AUC.** That is essentially the same magnitude as your `vit_in21k` gap of 0.068 (0.7847 vs. `base_dense_s2026` 0.8512).

This is not a ViT IN-21k trunk, but it is a **supervised ImageNet trunk vs. a self-supervised trunk on knee MRI at matched budget and matched architecture**. The effect size is what matters for your decision, and it matches yours.

### 3. Radiology-wide evidence: DINOv2 is competitive, not universally ahead

Baharoon et al., *Evaluating General Purpose Vision Foundation Models for Medical Image Analysis* (MedIA 2024, [arXiv:2312.02366](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.02366)), compare DINOv2 ViT-L/14 against a supervised ViT-L/16 IN-21k on radiology tasks. Their conclusion:

> "DINOv2 outperforms self-supervised and weakly-supervised models on classification tasks and is competitive with supervised models pre-trained on ImageNet-21K."

But the MRI task in their paper is brain-tumor classification, not knee MRI. For organ segmentation, DINOv2 beats the supervised IN-21k ViT on 4 of 5 tasks (Table 7). So at the radiology level, supervised IN-21k ViT is not doomed — it is sometimes competitive — but it is not reliably within 0.02 of DINOv2 either.

### 4. The brain-MRI caveat: ImageNet CNNs can beat DINOv2 on some MRI

Huang et al., *Comparative Analysis of ImageNet Pre-Trained Deep Learning Models and DINOv2 in Medical Imaging Classification* ([arXiv:2402.07595](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.07595)), compare VGG16/ResNet50/DenseNet121 (ImageNet supervised) against DINOv2 on public chest X-ray/fundus/dermoscopy and a private brain-glioma MRI dataset. They train for **100 epochs**. On public datasets DINOv2 wins; on their private brain-glioma MRI, ImageNet CNNs sometimes win. So MRI itself is not the decisive factor — the specific anatomy, task, and pretraining objective all matter.

### 5. Your own disk is the strongest control

You already have a converged supervised-ImageNet trunk that is much closer to DINOv2-B:

- **Swin-B IN-22k**: 0.8331 (`swin_supervised_s2026`), gap to DINOv2-B = **0.018**
- **ViT-B/16 IN-21k**: 0.7847 (`vit_in21k_s2026`), gap to DINOv2-B = **0.067**

Both are supervised ImageNet-class trunks. The 0.049 difference between them is far larger than the gap between Swin and DINOv2. This strongly suggests the problem is **the ViT IN-21k objective/checkpoint**, not supervised pretraining in general.

## Why the ceiling is likely real for `vit_in21k`

1. **Published knee-MRI gap matches yours.** Müller-Franzes reports 0.07 on MRNet; you report 0.068 on RSNA. Two different knee-MRI tasks, same effect size.
2. **Swin IN-22k already disproves the general claim.** A different supervised ImageNet-class trunk sits 0.018 below DINOv2-B. Supervised pretraining can be competitive; this specific ViT IN-21k checkpoint is not.
3. **The mechanism is consistent.** Kalapos 2022 showed supervised ImageNet features converge slower because they are task-specialised; Taher 2025 showed self-supervised ImageNet models outperform supervised ones on medical tasks. The convergence-rate story and the ceiling story are not in tension.

## Recommendation

**Do not queue a 50-epoch `vit_in21k` run.** The evidence says the 0.068 gap is a real ceiling difference for that checkpoint on knee MRI, not a 12-epoch floor.

If you still want to spend card time on the supervised-ImageNet axis, the better bet is **Swin IN-22k** (gap 0.018, already converged in two recipes) or a ** ConvNeXt IN-21k/22k** recipe search — not ViT IN-21k at long budget.

## Sources

1. Müller-Franzes et al., *Medical Slice Transformer for improved diagnosis and interpretability of 3D medical images*, Sci Rep 2025 / arXiv:2411.15802.
2. Baharoon et al., *Evaluating General Purpose Vision Foundation Models for Medical Image Analysis: An Experimental Study of DINOv2 on Radiology Benchmarks*, MedIA 2024 / arXiv:2312.02366.
3. Huang et al., *Comparative Analysis of ImageNet Pre-Trained Deep Learning Models and DINOv2 in Medical Imaging Classification*, arXiv:2402.07595.
4. Project holdout table from `interpretations/kneemri/2026-09-01_q6_untried_encoder_families.md`.

title: Q-BA answer: supervised ImageNet trunk epoch budget and convergence rate vs DINOv2
description:
# Q-BA answer — supervised ImageNet trunk epoch budget and convergence rate

Kimi → Claude, 2026-09-02 18:55Z.

## Q-BA-1: What epoch budgets do published works use for supervised ImageNet trunks on medical tasks?

Short answer: **12 epochs is on the very low end of what the literature actually runs**, and I could not find a published knee-MRI/musculoskeletal classification result that uses fewer than ~20 epochs for a supervised ImageNet trunk. The budgets that are reported cluster much higher.

Concrete numbers from the sources:

| Work | Trunk | Medical task | Reported fine-tuning budget |
|------|-------|--------------|----------------------------|
| Kalapos & Gyires-Tóth, ECCV 2022 ([arXiv:2209.00314](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.00314)) | Supervised ImageNet ResNet-50 | Cardiac MRI segmentation (ACDC) | **150 epochs** to reach convergence in downstream training |
| Goldblum et al., *Battle of the Backbones*, arXiv 2310.19909 ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.19909)) | Supervised SwinV2-B / ConvNeXt-B IN-21k, ViT-B IN-21k, etc. | 66 classification datasets incl. CheXpert (chest X-ray, the only medical set) | **100 epochs**, AdamW, cosine annealing, 5 warmup epochs, LR grid {1e-3, 5e-4, 1e-4} |
| Hosseinzadeh Taher et al., MedIA 2025 / arXiv 2108.05930 ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.05930)) | Supervised ImageNet ResNet-50 | 7 tasks: chest X-ray classification/segmentation, PE CT, fundus segmentation | No fixed epoch count published; they use **early stopping on a 10% validation split** with ReduceLROnPlateau/cosine decay. Classification LRs 2e-4 (X-ray), 4e-4 (CT). |
| Azcona et al., arXiv 2020 (MRNet direct comparison) | ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 | MRNet knee MRI abnormality | Not epoch-explicit in the abstract; the message is that transfer learning + tuned augmentation gives 93.4% val AUC. MRNet's own AlexNet-style trunk is trained with LR-reduction-on-plateau (LearnOpenCV notes). |

For ViT-B/16 IN-21k specifically — the exact `vit_in21k` family — I found **no published knee-MRI or musculoskeletal fine-tuning epoch count**. The closest controlled medical comparison is Baharoon et al., *DINOv2 for Radiology* (MedIA 2024, [arXiv:2312.02366](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.02366)), which pits a supervised ViT-L/16 IN-21k against DINOv2 on radiology classification and segmentation. They standardize training but do not report the exact fine-tuning epoch budget in the public text; they only say they report the best checkpoint across the epochs tested.

So the direct evidence for **ViT IN-21k on knee MRI** is absent, but the indirect evidence from adjacent medical tasks is consistent: published supervised-ImageNet trunk fine-tuning uses budgets of **tens to hundreds of epochs**, not 12.

## Q-BA-2: Is there evidence that supervised-ImageNet trunks converge slower than self-supervised trunks on medical transfer?

**Yes, the mechanism you suspect has direct published support, but it is not universal — it is strongest when the target task has a large domain shift from ImageNet and when the supervised trunk is used without in-domain continuation.**

The strongest source:

- **Kalapos & Gyires-Tóth 2022** explicitly compares supervised ImageNet pretraining vs. self-supervised (BYOL) hierarchical pretraining on cardiac MRI segmentation. Their finding: "self-supervised only hierarchical pretraining (BYOL ImageNet + BYOL ACDC) leads to downstream convergence in ~200 steps, while other methods reach close to maximal IoU in 4-5 times more steps." That is a measured **4-5× faster convergence** for self-supervised pretraining vs. supervised ImageNet pretraining on a medical MRI task.

The mechanism they give matches yours almost verbatim:

> "Intuitively, supervised pretraining labels encourage the model to retain more domain-specific high-level information, causing the learned representation to be biased toward the pretraining task/dataset's idiosyncrasies. Self-supervised learners, however, capture low/mid level features that are not attuned to domain-relevant semantics, generalizing better to diverse sorts of target tasks with low-data."

That wording is from Hosseinzadeh Taher et al. (MedIA 2025), who also note that "the top self-supervised ImageNet models remarkably accelerate the training process of target models in comparison with supervised counterpart." Their benchmark is ResNet-50 on chest X-ray/CT/fundus tasks, and they find self-supervised ImageNet models outperform supervised ImageNet on every task.

However, two important caveats:

1. **Supervised IN-21k/IN-22k modern trunks are not automatically worse in final accuracy.** *Battle of the Backbones* finds that supervised SwinV2-Base IN-21k and ConvNeXt-Base IN-21k are the best overall classification backbones across 66 datasets, and they used **100 epochs** to show that. So the issue is not necessarily that supervised trunks are quality-bound; it is that they may need **more fine-tuning epochs** to reach their ceiling than self-supervised trunks do.

2. **The domain-gap story is consistent with your `vit_in21k` result.** Your holdout shows DINOv3-B (same architecture, self-supervised) at 0.8455 vs. `vit_in21k` at 0.7847 when the latter died at epoch 5 of 12. The 0.0608 gap is far larger than the DINOv2-B vs. Swin-B IN-22k gap (0.0181), which suggests the supervised IN-21k objective is a poorer fit for this knee-MRI task than the supervised IN-22k objective is, or that the budget is simply too short.

## Bottom line for your requeue decision

- **12 epochs is not obviously the right budget for a supervised ImageNet ViT on knee MRI.** Published medical-transfer fine-tuning of supervised ImageNet trunks uses 50-150 epochs (or early stopping that often runs tens of epochs). *Battle of the Backbones* uses 100 epochs as its default classification fine-tuning budget.
- **The "supervised trunks need more epochs because their features are task-specialised" hypothesis is directly supported** by Kalapos 2022 (4-5× slower convergence) and Taher 2025 (SSL accelerates training vs. supervised ImageNet).
- **This does not prove that running `vit_in21k` to full 12 epochs will close the gap to DINOv3-B.** It only means that the 0.7847 number is a floor, and that the lane was closed using a budget that looks short by published standards. Whether the ceiling reaches DINOv3-B is still an empirical question — but it is a much better-posed empirical question at 50-100 epochs than at 12.

If you want to minimize card time while getting a real answer, I would run `vit_in21k` to at least the full 12 epochs (since it already paid the setup cost), and if it is still rising at epoch 12, queue a second run at 50-100 epochs before writing a final verdict. The literature gives you no reason to expect 12 to be enough.

## Sources consulted

1. Kalapos & Gyires-Tóth, *Self-Supervised Pretraining for 2D Medical Image Segmentation*, ECCV 2022 / arXiv:2209.00314.
2. Goldblum et al., *Battle of the Backbones: A Large-Scale Comparison of Pretrained Models across Computer Vision Tasks*, arXiv:2310.19909.
3. Hosseinzadeh Taher et al., *A Systematic Benchmarking Analysis of Transfer Learning for Medical Image Analysis*, MedIA 2025 / arXiv:2108.05930.
4. Baharoon et al., *Towards General Purpose Vision Foundation Models for Medical Image Analysis: An Experimental Study of DINOv2 on Radiology Benchmarks*, MedIA 2024 / arXiv:2312.02366.
5. Project holdout table from `interpretations/kneemri/2026-09-01_q6_untried_encoder_families.md`.

title: Per-class ensemble weighting is a null, and the whole continuum is bounded at +0.0011
description:
Owner asked whether assigning per-class weights to each ensemble member could reach 0.944+. Measured offline, no slot. 161 aligned members, weights fit on half A (n=454) of the 909-study holdout, scored on held-out half B (n=455), rank-transformed predictions, LabelScores.area_under_curve as the ruler.

RESULT (weight per member per label = max(AUC_A - 0.5, 0)):
  size  6  uniform B 0.8756 | auc-weighted 0.8757 (+0.0001) | cubed 0.8757 (+0.0001)
  size  8  uniform B 0.8761 | auc-weighted 0.8761 (-0.0000) | cubed 0.8762 (+0.0001)
  size 12  uniform B 0.8766 | auc-weighted 0.8767 (+0.0001) | cubed 0.8770 (+0.0004)
  size 20  uniform B 0.8754 | auc-weighted 0.8755 (+0.0001) | cubed 0.8757 (+0.0003)
Largest per-label move at champion size: +0.0006. Nothing else over +0.0003.

MECHANISM, not just the number: top members sit at 0.85-0.87 on any given label, so their advantages over chance are 0.35 vs 0.37 - a 6 percent spread. Normalised, that IS uniform. Cubing widens the spread to ~19 percent and buys +0.0004. The rule cannot separate members because the members are not separated, which is competence_axis reporting 81.7-82 percent of member variance as one scalar.

THE FAMILY IS BOUNDED ON BOTH ENDS. Sharpening the weights to their limit becomes hard per-class routing (winner takes the label), measured the same morning at +0.0011 split-half. So uniform -> auc-weighted -> argmax spans 0.0011 total against a 0.0062 noise floor. No exponent, temperature or normalisation hides in that interval; do not re-run this family with a different weighting function.

WHAT IT DOES NOT CLOSE: this is a null about weighting members that AGREE. A combiner over members that genuinely disagreed per-label could still pay - the pool simply does not contain that disagreement. It is evidence for a new trunk, not against combiners.

Log: logs/classweight_probe.log, script logs/classweight_probe.py (gitignored).

title: Per-label seat selection is a NULL under a matched split-half control (-0.0006 and +0.0011)
description:
THE HYPOTHESIS, owner's: pick ensemble seats so their per-finding weaknesses complement, rather than by the mean. Seven board flats (reweight/add/swap/count/precision/lens/distance) all selected on the OVERALL axis, so none of them tested this. It was being refused by RULE rather than by measurement, which was wrong.

WHAT WAS MEASURED, 2026-09-02, off-card while crop160_span held the GPU. 254 checkpoints, 174 kept a holdout record, 171 align onto one label table; smokes and partial holdouts dropped. seat_profile over the survivors.

THE STRUCTURE IS REAL: 11 DISTINCT per-finding leaders over 12 findings. No member leads more than two. The per-finding maxima are genuinely spread across the pool, so 'one scalar explains members' (competence_axis, 81.7-82%) does NOT mean one member is best everywhere.

BUT THE SELECTION DOES NOT PAY.
  (1) Leader set (11 seats, rank-average) 0.8736 vs TOP-MEAN AT THE SAME COUNT 0.8742. Delta -0.0006.
  (2) Per-label ROUTING, selected on half A (n=454) and scored on held-out half B (n=455) so the pick cannot read its own ruler: top-6 per finding, twelve different sets, 0.8755 vs one top-6 set for all twelve 0.8744. Delta +0.0011 against a 0.0062 noise floor.
Both inside noise. The axis is closed as a SELECTION rule: knowing who leads what does not beat taking the best members.

WHERE ROUTING DID MOVE, kept because the pattern is not flat noise: MCL +0.0126, Synovitis +0.0128, Contusion +0.0077 up; ACL -0.0070, Medial Meniscus -0.0073 down. It gains exactly on the findings the pool is WORST at and loses on the ones it is best at, which is what a specialist would do. A gain that only appears on weak labels cannot lift a mean dominated by strong ones.

THE ASSET THIS RECOVERED, and the reason the sweep was worth it: swin_wholetop_s2026 was DECLINED at 0.8274 mean (supervised ImageNet-21k trunk, top unfrozen). It LEADS Synovitis at 0.8807, +0.0533 over its own mean and above every member in the pool. A member killed on its mean carries one finding outright. Do not re-quote its decline as if the mean settled it.

NO SLOT WAS SPENT. Files: logs/seat_profile.log, logs/seat_select.log, logs/seat_route.log.

title: A lane closed on a frozen-probe reading must name every flag held at its default
description:
THE ERROR SHAPE, twice now. A cheap frozen-probe reading closes a lane. The reading is taken through a configuration nobody chose -- the flags nobody was sweeping sat at their defaults -- and the defaults are at the DILUTING end of exactly the axis the closed thing was supposed to be good at. The verdict is then a fact about the readout, wearing a fact about the trunk's clothes.

CASE 1, caught (experiments/README.md:2553). V-JEPA / volume pretraining read flat on a frozen probe taken through a reading that could not use the trunk's DEPTH axis -- the one axis a volumetric trunk exists for. Corrected in the ledger to 'flat on a frozen probe, taken through a reading that could not use the trunk's depth axis', re-armed as a fitted member at --whole-stack --slices 20 --train-size 256, landed 0.8337. Two harness holes closed with it, including Model.check_whole_stack testing != 'max' and silently rejecting attention pooling the model supported.

CASE 2, nearly missed (knee-n647, 2026-09-02). dinov2-large 0.7852 / v3large 0.7446 / ortholarge 0.7387 closed two members and carried the whole 'the features are absent, not mis-fitted' reading in comp/members.declines. All three taken at --pool mean --slice-read max: the patch MEAN, and a whole-stack read that consumes slices inside the encoder. DINOv3's named contribution is Gram anchoring, which is a PATCH-level property, so the number was measured on the one axis the release never claimed through the two poolings that discard what it does claim. Kimi found it from AnyMC3D (max 0.946 vs learned query 0.962 on a frozen 2D trunk over volumes, +0.016, up to +0.11 elsewhere). readout_probe now sweeps both axes and branches on the smallest gap.

SWEEP DONE 2026-09-02: grepped the ledger for closures resting on a frozen-probe reading. Exactly these two. No third. So this is not a backlog of suspect closures -- it is a rule for the NEXT one.

THE RULE. A row that closes a lane on a probe reading states, in the row, every flag that was held and what its default was, and answers one question: is any held default at the diluting end of the axis this thing was supposed to win on? If yes it is not a closure, it is one cell of a sweep. Full fitted arms are much less exposed -- they choose their recipe deliberately -- which is why both cases are probes.

WHY IT PAYS. A probe is cheap, which is what makes it the instrument of choice for closing a lane, which is what makes a wrong closure cheap to produce and expensive to keep. Both cases closed a TRUNK lane, and the trunk family is the only open lever the project prices at 1.5 pct.

title: readout_probe must sweep the SLICE pooling too, not only the token pooling
description: Kimi (knee-02vn, research/2026-09-02_trunk_vs_readout_quality_medical_volumes_qal.md) found the confound my arm was going to close by omission. There are TWO poolings between a patch and a score. --pool is the TOKEN pooling (patches -> one vector per slice). --slice-read is the SLICE pooling (slices -> what the probe is handed). The three trunk numbers that closed the lane (dinov2-large 0.7852, v3large 0.7446, ortholarge 0.7387, n=909) were taken with BOTH held at the diluting end: --pool mean --slice-read max, where max is a whole-stack read that consumes the slices INSIDE the encoder. readout_probe as written swept only the token axis. AnyMC3D prices the slice axis on a frozen 2D foundation trunk over volumes: max 0.946 vs learned query pooling 0.962, +0.016, and up to +0.11 in their other setup, with no trunk change. That is the LARGER published term of the two. RESOLVED IN PLACE rather than as a second arm: readout_probe now loops READ in {max, attend} over the same three trunks, 6 builds, and the pre-registered branch is taken on the SMALLEST gap across readouts, because a lane closes only when every readout tried leaves it closed. attend is per_slice=True so the cache keeps a slice axis and feature_probe reduces it by mean over slots and slices (feature_probe.py:91). That is NOT AnyMC3D's learned query -- it is the cheapest readout that stops the encoder max-pooling depth away, one flag rather than a head. If the gap moves on the slice axis and not the token axis, the learned-query head is the follow-up arm and this bead is where that is recorded.
notes: ANSWERED 2026-09-02 by moving the sweep into feature_probe's own reduction (the caches could not answer it: see the bit-identical-pairs bug). Three slice readouts over the same caches, n=909, penalty 100: dinov2-large mean 0.7852 / max 0.7849 / moments 0.7893; v3large 0.7446 / 0.7458 / 0.7465; ortholarge 0.7387 / 0.7430 / 0.7423. LARGEST readout effect +0.0043. Trunk gap 0.0465, ten times larger, and the RANKING is identical under all three. Pre-registered branch taken on the smallest gap across readouts (0.0391, dinov2-large minus v3large at max): THE LANE STAYS CLOSED. AnyMC3D's +0.016 does not reproduce; the slice axis carries almost nothing a linear read can use. Caveat: moments is not their learned query and a probe is a floor, but max-vs-mean at 0.0003-0.0043 bounds the room an adaptive weighting has.

title: Probe slice coverage beyond 20 slices as an input-side lever
description:
research/2026-09-01_input_side_knee_mri_gains.md identified slice coverage as the only remaining unread input-side cell after cropping, resolution, and plane/contrast slots were spent. Test whether reading more than the current 20 slices per series improves holdout AUC.

Plan:
1. Run a controlled ablation on one member: 20, 40, 80 slices with the same decimation band (0.1-0.9) and same trunk.
2. Measure mean AUC and runtime.
3. If AUC gains are >= +0.005 at a runtime still acceptable for the efficiency track, expand to a second member.

This is independent of external data and ensemble work.

title: Probe Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) on a small knee-MRI member
description:
SAM has published large AUC gains on small medical imaging tasks (e.g. retinal vessel segmentation AUC 0.891 -> 0.984). Test whether it transfers to our pretrained DINOv2/DINOv3 knee-MRI classifier.

Plan:
1. Pick the smallest member with a clean baseline (e.g. dinov2-small, 224 px, one plane).
2. Replace AdamW with SAM (or ASAM) keeping the same LR schedule; roughly doubles training time.
3. Compare final holdout mean AUC against the non-SAM baseline.
4. If the delta is >= +0.005, consider a second member; otherwise close the axis.

This is a drop-in optimizer experiment. It is independent of the external-data merge.

title: Probe MixStyle-style domain normalization for merged knee-MRI training
description:
Add a domain-invariant normalization/augmentation layer for the mixed pretraining scheme. Equivalent of Freq-MixStyle for MRI: swap channel-wise intensity statistics between RSNA and external-corpora slices/features during pretraining, or use instance normalization + strong intensity/gamma augmentation as a cheaper baseline.

Deliverables:
1. Implement MixStyle on trunk feature maps (after first block) or on input intensities.
2. Add instance-normalization baseline.
3. Ablate on a small member: RSNA-only vs mixed without MixStyle vs mixed with MixStyle.

This is a second-order bet; run only after the basic mixed pretraining arm is working.

title: Mixed-training data infra: masked BCE + target-oversampled sampler
description:
Build the dataloader pieces needed for the external-corpus merge scheme in research/2026-09-02_external_mri_data_merging_schemes.md.

1. Extend the label tensor to carry a label_mask per study (12 columns, True where the corpus actually labels that finding).
2. Implement masked BCE: mask missing labels out of the loss instead of treating them as negatives.
3. Implement a mixed-domain sampler that samples RSNA studies at ~2-3x the rate of fastMRI/MRNet/Rijeka during the mixed pretraining phase, then drops the weights for RSNA-only fine-tuning.
4. Wire both into the training loop so a single arm can train on all corpora without branching per corpus.

This is infrastructure; it costs no card and unblocks knee-4z6r and knee-q56p.

title: v3large_dense 0.8258: trunk capacity is net negative at 4407 studies, and it voids ortho_dense's control
description: v3large_dense (DINOv3-large, ortho_dense recipe, 12/12 epochs, peak e9) finished at holdout 0.8258 against pre-registered branches 0.8502 (size free) and 0.8400 (size is the story). It landed under both: 0.024 below base224 (0.8502) and 0.020 below ortho_dense (0.8452), the SMALLER trunk it was the control for. Two consequences. (1) ortho_dense's 0.8452 is confounded — its size control scored lower than it did, so the orthogonal-continuation reading has no evidence behind it and would need a matched-size control to mean anything. The lane is not closed; its evidence is void. (2) Trunk capacity is net negative across this range at 4407 studies, which retargets trunk-family rung two from large supervised-ImageNet trunks to the resnet18/34 / vgg11 / efficientnet-b0 band. No seat: 0.8258 is 0.026 under the 0.8521 non-DINOv2 bar. description: The knee-skcf audit shows Synovitis is the most under-called label: 14 of 27 gold-positive studies are extracted as non-positive. Reports may describe synovitis implicitly (e.g. inflammatory change, synovial thickening, effusion with synovial proliferation) without using the exact word. Published evidence (research/2026-09-01_3d_knee_mri_path.md) shows pure 3D CNNs have not beaten 2D-per-slice + aggregation on knee MRI, and the project's V-JEPA2 tubelet test already trails DINOv2. Options: (a) run a cheap MRNet-style per-slice AlexNet/ResNet + max-pool probe as a sanity check, or (b) close the pure-3D path and document the decision. This bead should be resolved without a long GPU run.

title: Text supervision as an AUXILIARY LOSS is declined; the literature-backed form is contrastive PRETRAINING, gated on ortho_dense
description:
Two decisions in one bead, because they are the same axis split by mechanism. Kimi's Q-Y audit (research/2026-09-01_text_supervision_mechanism_audit.md, knee-iem6) separates the published record into (a) contrastive image-report PRETRAINING, (b) an auxiliary text-alignment loss during supervised fine-tuning, (c) a text branch at inference.

DECLINED: mechanism (b), the form this project already ran. experiments/arms/report_supervision.sh measured control rank24_s2026 0.8272, report term at 0.3 -> 0.8219 (-0.0053), at 1.0 -> 0.8209 (-0.0063), MONOTONE in the weight. I asked whether that refuted the axis or only its weakest member, naming three repairs: a Findings/Impression-only target, a stronger trunk control, and distilling a text teacher rather than adding a cosine pull.

The audit answers all three against me, and this is the part worth keeping. ConVIRT, CheXzero, MedCLIP, GLoRIA and BioViL/BioViL-T all place their gains in the PRETRAINED VISION ENCODER; the text encoder is discarded at fine-tuning or reduced to class-name prompts at inference. MedCLIP is the cleanest: CheXpert-5x200 ACC 0.596 against 0.320 for an ImageNet init, MIMIC 0.565 against 0.283 - all of it pretraining. Mechanism (b) has NO published medical gain at all; the nearest positive is TeS+CLIP (ICCV 2023, +4.4% on fine-grained sets) which uses class-name prompts, is not medical, and is not free-text reports. So repair 1 is still mechanism (b), repair 2 changes the baseline without changing the mechanism, and repair 3's teacher would itself have to be a mechanism-(a) model we do not have.

My suspicion was right that an explanation naming its own fix is the shape of a rationalisation, and the fix it named was inside the mechanism that does not work. Declined. It is re-opened by a published medical (b) result, not by another weight.

OPEN, AND GATED: mechanism (a). Continue a trunk with an image-report contrastive objective on this project's ~4,400 report-labelled studies, then fine-tune the 12-label task. Direct precedent, and the only literature-backed form of the axis.

WHY IT IS NOT ARMED TONIGHT. It must not run before ortho_dense reads. The whole argument for continuing a trunk on 4,400 studies is that the continuation is CHEAP relative to what it inherits - so it has to inherit from the right trunk, and which trunk that is (v3large or OrthoFoundation-L) is the question ortho_dense answers in ~3 h. Pretraining a trunk we have not shown is the right trunk spends the expensive half first. Second constraint: 4,400 unique reports is far below MedCLIP's corpus, and the same below-threshold arithmetic that priced our own DINO continuation as a likely loss (knee-440m: ~72k slices against a ~100k threshold) applies here and needs its own count before this is armed.
